title: Wired to Steal:  The Behavioral Production of the Colonizer
author: Yoav Litvin
content:

to-steal-the-behavioral-production-of-the-colonizer/)

Image courtesy Yoav Litvin.

_“The only possibility of regaining one 's balance is to face the whole
problem, for all these discoveries, all these inquiries lead only in one
direction: to make man admit that he is nothing, absolutely nothing—and that
he must put an end to the narcissism on which he relies in order to imagine
that he is different from the other “animals.””_

~Frantz Fanon, _Black Skin, White Masks_ (trans. Charles Lam Markmann, Grove
Press, 1967)

Frantz Fanon (1925-1961), the Martinican psychiatrist, political philosopher
and revolutionary thinker, provided invaluable insight into the minds of the
colonizer and the colonized. Writing through the lens of colonial violence,
Fanon delineated the psychological wounds inflicted on the oppressed with
brutal precision and moral urgency. In _The_ _Wretched of the Earth_ (1961)
and _Black Skin, White Masks_(1952), he detailed how colonialism dehumanizes
both oppressor and oppressed, albeit in different ways, destroys and then
constructs identity, sustains a sense of inferiority, and ultimately produces
submission. Crucially, Fanon implicated a phenomenon among colonized people
who, in a bid to reclaim agency, redirect aggression downward in the hierarchy
of colonized society, thereby reinforcing the oppressive structure.

Fanon's insight rested on a crucial scientific reality: stripped of the
narcissistic exceptionalism manufactured by colonial structures, the human
animal is subject to the same behavioral and neurological mechanisms as other
social mammals. “Regaining one’s balance” is contingent on dismantling this
construct.

Fanon's notions, together with more recent contributions of scholars such as
[Lara Sheehi](https://www.plutobooks.com/product/from-the-clinic-to-the-
streets/), whose psychoanalytic work investigates colonial subjectivity, and
[Samah Jabr](https://drsamahjabr.com/#latest-book), whose complementary
clinical work explores the psychological realities of occupation and
resistance, correspond with what W.E.B. Du Bois (1868–1963), the American
sociologist, historian and activist who pioneered the study of race as a
structural rather than biological phenomenon, called a "public and
psychological wage": the social status, deference and institutional privileges
conferred by racial belonging which bind the most economically marginal in-
group members to the hierarchy rather than to those below them (_Black
Reconstruction in America_ , 1935).

Several thinkers have further shed light on the potential motivations behind
cruelty and subjugation, though their focus has fallen more on how ordinary
people become capable of violence than on the structural dynamics of
oppressive systems themselves. These include, among others, Hannah Arendt's
(1906-1975) analysis of how ordinary people can perpetuate atrocity within a
bureaucratic system; Erich Fromm's (1900-1980) analysis of aggression and the
psychological structures authoritarian societies produce; Stanley Milgram’s
(1933-1984) experiments, which showed how readily people inflict pain on
others when instructed by an authority figure; Philip Zimbardo's (1933-2024)
account of how institutional power can convert ordinary people into punitive
sadists; and James Waller's (1961-) extension into behaviors during genocidal
events, including dehumanization, in-group preference, and moral indifference
toward atrocity.

What remains inadequately addressed is the behavioral and neurological
architecture through which colonial violence is produced, transmitted, and
sustained.

**The Wired to Steal model**

The W2S model presents a novel neurobehavioral framework. Drawing on
neuroscience and evolutionary biology, it analyses propaganda and rhetoric as
instruments of conditioning that service domination and recruitment, rather
than accepting them at face value and thus reproducing them. It identifies
which behavioral dynamics recur across settler colonial projects, how ruling
classes mobilize entire populations as accomplices, and how systems of power
perpetuate theft and inequality by manipulating psychological drives.
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Screen-
Shot-2026-08-24-at-9.39.28-AM-680x1016.png)](https://interlinkbooks.com/product/wired-
to-steal/)

The model proposes that greed drives a self-reinforcing, escalatory cycle in
which manufactured identity, fearmongering, selective privilege, and
conditioning to aggression, produced through intermittent reinforcement,
enable genocide as a means of dispossession. Violence escalates, then
normalizes with consistency and efficiency, until entire societies are
destroyed.

What drives warfare associated with colonial expansionism and how are entire
populations recruited to serve agendas which benefit only a privileged few?
What distinguishes those who resist from those who comply or become active
perpetrators? How are colonial narratives constructed and systematically
maintained to override empathy? And perhaps most critically, under what
conditions does the cycle break, and what does behavioral science inform us
about dismantling the colonial psychology, in individuals and in societies?

Addressing these questions first requires examining the nature of warfare
itself.

**The origins of human warfare**

War is a form of violent social aggression. Unlike interpersonal violence or
homicide, war involves organized, cooperative and often armed conflict,
sanctioned by societies and waged by one group against another with the intent
to kill. In its basic form, warfare is a political instrument in which
coalitions collaborate aggressively to seize and defend resources vital for
reproduction.

Is warfare an expression of “human nature,” a collective behavior rooted in
early human or even primate ancestry, or is it a relatively recent cultural
construct which emerged with the development of modern human societies?

The question reaches back millions of years in evolutionary history, yet
carries profound implications for modern life, human well-being and the future
of humanity and the planet.

If war is indeed human nature, then understanding it requires a thorough
investigation of human evolutionary history and perhaps that of our primate
ancestors. Overcoming the injustices of war would mean the daunting task of
transcending our own innate programming. If, however, it is a recent cultural
construct, then examining its origins may reveal pathways to mitigate and
perhaps even dismantle this phenomenon in the pursuit of a more just and
equitable society.

Historically, reactionaries have promoted the notion that war is innate,
making colonial violence appear inevitable rather than constructed, thus
disguising their culpability. Further, it has been used to justify domination
and expansionism and villainize resistance by falsely depicting Indigenous
peoples as violent savages who may benefit from subjugation “for their own
good.”

The[ available evidence](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/war-is-
not-part-of-human-nature/), however, points elsewhere.

Comparative studies of mammals, including non-human primates, do not support
the idea of sustained, organized warfare as an innate collective behavior.
Archaeological and anthropological research on early human societies, as well
as ethnographic studies of existing hunter-gatherer groups, similarly suggest
that large-scale, coordinated collective violence is not a universal feature
of human societies.

Though not universally accepted and subject to ongoing debate, the weight of
evidence indicates war is a relatively modern cultural construct. War emerged
around 10,000-12,000 years ago during the transition from migratory hunter-
gatherer collectives to sedentary lifestyles involving agriculture, animal
domestication and pastoralism, which enabled the accumulation of resources and
consequent emergence of social inequalities (the Neolithic Revolution).

War is not inevitable. It is a ruling class construct driven by greed and
resource accumulation, and thus the engine of the W2S model. Yet greed alone
does not explain how colonial violence operates on the ground. For that
purpose, we need to examine the two forms of aggression the ruling class
deploys and why their duplicitous conflation promotes colonial aims.

**Defense and offense: the behavioral manifestations of war**

Throughout the animal world, aggression manifests in two forms: defensive and
offensive. Though these forms appear similar to the untrained eye and are thus
frequently conflated, defensive and offensive aggression are driven by
different motivations and serve distinct purposes.

Defensive aggression originates from fear, while offensive aggression with
control and domination. Defense is typically directed at eliminating threats,
as when prey responds to a predator, and offense at subduing opponents within
a hierarchy, as when two animals vie for dominance. Defensive aggression may
be lethal because it is motivated byֿֿ survival by any means necessary.
Offensive aggression is typically oriented toward submission, not death of an
opponent because hierarchies depend on preserving membership.

Defensive and offensive aggression also differ in their neurobiological and
neuroendocrine correlates. Defensive aggression activates systems associated
with fear and survival, including stress hormones (e.g. glucocorticoids) and
fear-related neural circuits. Offensive aggression engages systems associated
with dominance, reward and sociality, including testosterone and dopaminergic
pathways.

These two forms of aggression have independent neural circuitries,
neurotransmitters and hormonal profiles. Conflating them, as colonial
propaganda consistently does, obscures the nature of the violence being
committed and its ruling class origins.

**The W2S behavioral cycle**

Colonizers deploy both forms simultaneously. Greed, which is addictive through
repeated rewards, drives a ruling class to employ offensive aggression as a
means of theft, manufacturing a tribal collective identity which demarcates
in- and out-group boundaries. The in-group enjoys the fruits of social
belonging and the theft of land, resources and labor; the out-group is
excluded, exploited and ultimately eliminated. Fear and the defensive
aggression it produces in the dispossessed is then reframed as existential
necessity, justifying the oppression and dispossession that greed initiated.

Because most humans naturally feel empathy toward others and broad populations
are reticent to sacrifice themselves, their families, friends and resources
for the interests of a privileged few, offensive aggression is rarely
sustainable on its own, particularly in collectivist versus individualistic
societies and in the post-WWII era of international law, where such aggression
is viewed as morally and legally indefensible. Ruling classes, therefore,
employ propaganda narratives to reframe offensive aggression as justifiable
lethal defense.

The European conquest (“discovery”) of “the New World” makes this plain: the
quest for riches came first and the narratives followed. Racial hierarchies,
manufactured identities, religious and ideological justifications, are all
engineered to serve continued resource extraction through segregation,
violence and suppression of empathy.

Colonial propaganda suppresses empathy through at least five mechanisms:
dehumanization — through religion, racism, economic rationalization (the claim
that Indigenous peoples were not making productive use of the land),
civilizational and developmental reasoning (the claim that Indigenous peoples
were at a lower stage of human development and required European tutelage), or
the portrayal of Native resistance as savage aggression — which lowers the
threshold for invader violence; threat inversion, which recasts the
dispossessed as aggressors; divine mandate, which removes moral agency and
lowers the bar for “permissible” violence; historical erasure, which denies
the out-group's existence and culture; and fear conditioning, which activates
defensive neural circuitry, making violence seem necessary.

Dehumanization changes who you see, threat inversion changes what you think
happened, divine mandate removes your choice for violence, historical erasure
removes the victim entirely, and fear conditioning changes how your nervous
system responds. They work together because they target different systems
simultaneously, making the whole more resistant to disruption than any single
mechanism would be.

In-group members who uphold the hierarchy through aggression are positively
rewarded across three simultaneous tracks: material gain, status, privilege
and other social rewards and the neurological pleasure of humiliating the out-
group (intergroup _schadenfreude_). Military service and periodic wars ensure
this schedule is reinforced across the population, not only in those who would
seek it out.

Within the in-group, investment in the oppressive structure, as well as
individualism, competition and consumption are promoted, keeping members
focused on personal accumulation and social positioning rather than collective
questioning of the structure itself. Those who dissent face exclusion,
demonization and ultimately threats to their physical safety, with fear of
these consequences keeping most of society in perpetual acquiescence.

Fanon observed that violence can function as a release valve, particularly
among the lower classes within the perpetrators' in-group hierarchy. The
stress physiology literature now explains why: colonial propaganda installs
chronic fear, producing sustained physiological stress that is attenuated by
redirecting aggression toward those perceived as lower in the social
hierarchy, particularly out-group members constructed as threats. This
behavior is negatively reinforced; it produces relief from an aversive state.
The same pattern is documented in social primates other than humans.

Repeated positive reward across all three domains, plus negative
reinforcement, delivered on intermittent schedules, produce a conditioned
appetite for violence that persists and escalates. This is the same mechanism
that makes slot machines highly addictive: variable-ratio reinforcement
schedules are the most powerful conditioning systems known, and the most
resistant to extinction (a process by which reward is withdrawn, and the
conditioned behavior ceases).

Violence is an essential tool to enforce an inherently unjust hierarchy, which
creates resistance by those it dispossesses. This violence can be direct,
whether military, police, or paramilitary force, or structural, embedded
within institutions that limit movement, access to resources or political
rights.

A greedy ruling class requires a population to engage in offensive aggression
to seize resources and accumulate wealth. Most people, however, have no stake
in that seizure. What’s more, natural empathy resists violence against those
who have done them no harm. The ruling class therefore reframes offensive
aggression as defensive necessity. To do so it manufactures identity,
constructing segregated in-group and out-groups, with the out-groups
designated for dispossession. Fearmongering, dehumanization and selective
reward then deepen the divide and justify the violence. When resistance
occurs, escalation follows, and each escalation, once normalized, becomes the
new baseline, feeding back into the conditions that serve greed. The cycle is
self-reinforcing and, without intervention, self-perpetuating, comparable to
dynamics of addiction.

Colonial systems reproduce themselves through three interlocking forces:
structural incentives, social normalization and neurological conditioning.
Legislation, media, education systems and promises of impunity
institutionalize aggression, while repeated fear and reward cycles normalize
violence across generations.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Screen-
Shot-2026-08-24-at-9.34.17-AM-680x372.png)

**Figure 1.** The Wired to Steal Model. The Wired to Steal model depicts a
self-reinforcing cycle through which systems of domination reproduce
themselves. Greed drives the pursuit of power and control over land and
resources. Societies are shaped through psychological conditioning, mobilizing
fear, identity and selective privilege and rewards, which produce hierarchical
social orders. These hierarchies are maintained through violence and coercion.
Over time, inequality becomes normalized through institutions, laws and
dominant narratives. This normalization reinforces the conditions that allow
greed to persist and grow, completing a positive feedback loop that
perpetuates the system across generations (Interlink Books; with permission).

**Why the model matters**

Conventional political and historical analyses treat colonial narratives as
alternate interpretations rather than as emotional recruitment and
normalization tools, that is, as arguments to be refuted rather than
conditioned responses to be understood and addressed. In doing so, they can
grant propaganda legitimacy, sustaining and even reinforcing the narratives it
seeks to challenge. Colonial narratives do not engage the reasoning areas of
the mind, they work on emotional centers of the nervous system, particularly
the relatively primitive fear and reward circuitries which determine what
feels true before any logical argument begins.

One would not argue rationally with Pavlov's dog to stop salivating. This is
not because the dog has no language skill, it is because the behavior was not
produced through reasoning. The same principle applies to humans with phobias:
no amount of rational persuasion can relieve them. What is necessary is
behavioral intervention targeting the conditioned response directly. Colonial
conditioning requires the same kind of intervention, such as exposure therapy,
in which gradual contact with the feared stimulus rewires the conditioned
response without the necessity of rational convincing.

W2S approaches colonial narratives as behavioral endpoints and tools serving
dispossession. By identifying greed as the primary driver, sustained and
escalated through intermittent reinforcement across manufactured identity,
social reward and conditioned aggression, as well as punishment of dissent,
the model distinguishes between offense by the colonizer aimed at control and
domination, which includes the construction and deployment of narratives, and
defense by the colonized, necessary for survival and protection of resources.
It explains how ruling classes manufacture violence for theft and how ordinary
people are recruited as accomplices.

Because the model is grounded in behavioral neuroscience and evolutionary
biology rather than the specifics of any single historical case, it identifies
recurring patterns across vastly different settler colonial contexts, making
it comparative, predictive, and considerably harder to dismiss as partisan. In
doing so, it dismantles propaganda, obstructs divide-and-conquer strategies,
and builds solidarity between all those oppressed by similar systems of
domination.

The W2S model clarifies why systems such as colonialism, apartheid, slavery
and other forms of authoritarian control can endure for generations, even when
their injustice becomes widely visible.

Further, the same framework also identifies where interventions can be useful.
Empathy is innate and moral disengagement is conditioned, and therefore
reversible. Those who resist can maintain or recover empathy circuits through
exposure to the humanity of the out-group, counter-narratives (such as W2S)
and alternative social community. Solidarity through co-resistance becomes the
neurological, behavioral antidote to the rewards and privileges the oppressive
system installs.

Further, the model points to empowerment of the oppressed, disruption of
segregation and propaganda narratives, and withdrawal of rewards, from within
and outside the system, as effective means of resistance. The histories of
anti-colonial resistance demonstrate that struggle and solidarity can reclaim
a humanity in which the liberation of the colonized frees the colonizer as
well. Disrupting the mechanisms outlined in the W2S model requires cultivating
their neurobehavioral opposites: sociality, critical education, and
intersectional solidarity as alternative rewards. This cultural transformation
must be grounded in real material needs, adaptive rather than rigid and led by
the oppressed.

**Zionism and Wired to Steal**

Each element of the W2S cycle is observable in Israeli expansionist and
genocidal behavior, before and since October 7th. Within the W2S framework,
the Zionist project is not exceptional. It follows a white supremacist dynamic
common across other settler-colonial projects, including the United States,
Australia, and South Africa.

The same cycle driven by greed is fully operational in Israel’s actions in
Gaza, the West Bank, Lebanon, Syria and Iran today. The actions of Israeli
Prime Minister Netanyahu and U.S. President Trump are natural expressions of a
ruling class which acts with impunity, while being perfectly aligned with and
enhancing the violent cycle the model describes.

Greed is expressed through systematic land and resource theft, including
looting; collective identity is organized through narratives of divine
entitlement; fear is stoked through the decontextualization of Hamas’s actions
as genocidal and uniquely sadistic; selective privilege rewards settlers with
land, status, and impunity while punishing dissent. The intermittent
reinforcement schedule propels the destruction of hospitals, photographing of
degraded prisoners, torture in myriad forms, the burning of olive groves, and
so many other atrocities; all acts that service displacement, terror and
genocide, consistent with a humiliation reward track conditioned through
decades of impunity.

Crucially, these behaviors are products of a constructed Zionist culture; they
are conditioned rather than expressions of innate human nature. Thus, these
same processes can be reversed, enabling populations to reconnect with their
shared humanity and capacity for empathy, laying a foundation for co-
resistance with Indigenous Palestinians against domination, genocide, and
theft.
